title: Water from the Rock and War with Amalek
summary: At Rephidim the people find no water, quarrel with Moses, and put the LORD to the test. God has Moses strike the rock at Horeb and water pours out, and the place is named Massah and Meribah. Then the Amalekites attack, and Israel prevails as long as Moses' hands are held up on the hilltop; afterward God orders a written memorial and Moses builds an altar called The LORD Is My Banner.
story: The sea is behind Israel (chapters 14-15), bitter water has been made sweet at Marah, and manna has fed the camp in the Desert of Sin (chapter 16). Each of those episodes follows the same pattern of need, complaint, and gift. Chapter 17 repeats the pattern with water and then breaks it with something new, an armed enemy. This is the last stretch of road before Sinai, where the covenant will be made in chapter 19. Two names that matter later enter the story here. Joshua, who will lead Israel into Canaan after Moses' death, appears for the first time as a field commander. Amalek becomes the archetypal enemy of God's people, remembered in Deuteronomy, fought by Saul and David, and echoed in the book of Esther, whose villain Haman is called an Agagite, a title Jewish tradition connects with Agag, the Amalekite king whom Saul spared.
historical:
Israel is in the wilderness between Egypt and Sinai, a few weeks after the exodus (the debate over its date is set out in the introduction to Exodus). Rephidim cannot be located with certainty. If Mount Sinai is the traditional Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, Rephidim lay in the valleys to its northwest, and the Wadi Feiran, the largest oasis in that region, is often suggested. Horeb, where the rock stands (verse 6), is the name Deuteronomy usually gives to Sinai, which suggests the camp was already in the region of the mountain of God.

The Amalekites were a nomadic people of the Negev and the Sinai. Genesis 36:12 traces them to Amalek, a grandson of Esau, which makes them distant kin of Israel. They recur throughout Israel's history: they rout Israel as far as Hormah (Numbers 14:45), raid alongside the Midianites in Gideon's day (Judges 6:3), are the target of Saul's campaign (1 Samuel 15), and burn David's town of Ziklag (1 Samuel 30). They are not clearly attested outside the Bible, which is unsurprising for a people who left no cities or inscriptions.
cultural:
Water in the Sinai comes from scattered springs and wells that a large company with flocks could quickly drain, so the thirst was real. What turns the complaint into an offense is its form. The people contend with Moses, using a verb at home in the lawcourt, and they test the LORD, demanding proof of what he has already shown them. Their question, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (verse 7), puts God on trial. Stoning, which Moses fears in verse 4, was execution carried out by the whole community, so his fear means the camp is turning on its leader.

On the hilltop Moses holds “the staff of God” (verse 9), the staff that struck the Nile, where the fighting men below can see it. The altar name in verse 15 uses nes, a signal pole raised on a height to rally troops. The scene does not present Moses' arms as a charm. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200, already asked whether Moses' hands won or lost the battle, and answered that Israel prevailed whenever the people looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven. The command to write the victory “on a scroll as a reminder” (verse 14) is the first time in the Bible that anyone is told to write something down.
literary: The chapter is two scenes joined by a place, Rephidim, and by the staff. In the first, the people quarrel and God provides; in the second, an enemy attacks and God fights. Each scene ends with a name: Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarreling) for the place of the water, and The LORD Is My Banner for the altar. The word hand runs through the battle like a thread: the staff in Moses' hand, his hands raised and lowered, the hands Aaron and Hur hold steady, and the hand lifted in verse 16. Verse 12 calls his hands emunah, steady, the word elsewhere translated faithfulness. Verse 16 is a compressed poetic oath. Its word kes occurs only here, and many scholars take it as a variant or miscopying of nes, banner, while others keep the sense throne, as the BSB does.

outline.t: No water at Rephidim, and the people quarrel
Water from the rock at Horeb: Massah and Meribah
Battle with Amalek while Moses' hands are held up
A written memorial and the altar The LORD Is My Banner

doctrines.note: God meets two threats in one chapter, thirst and a raiding army, and works through ordinary means both times: a staff, a rock, soldiers with swords. The outcome is still his, and his care does not wait until his complaining people deserve it.

The sin at Massah is not thirst or asking for water. It is testing God, demanding that he prove his presence on the people's terms after he has already shown it. Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3 hold up this scene as the pattern of a hardened heart.

Moses takes the crowd's fury to the LORD rather than answering it himself. His raised hands on the hill, which many interpreters read as a posture of prayer, show dependence on God, and his need for Aaron and Hur shows that even the one who intercedes must be held up by others.

words.note: Nasah, to test or put to the proof. In chapter 16 God tests Israel, to see whether they will follow his instructions (16:4), as he once tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1). Here Israel tests God, which reverses the proper order. The place name Massah comes from this root, and later Scripture uses it as shorthand for unbelief (Deuteronomy 6:16; Psalm 95:8).

Riv, to quarrel or contend, often in the sense of bringing a case against someone. The people file a complaint against Moses and, through him, against God. Meribah comes from the same root. The prophets later turn the word around, picturing the LORD bringing his own case against his people (Micah 6:2).

Nes, a banner or signal pole set on a height to rally troops. Moses names the altar The LORD Is My Banner: Israel's rallying point in battle is God himself. The same word names the pole that holds the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:8) and the signal the LORD raises for the nations in Isaiah 11:10-12.

christ: Paul reads this chapter in 1 Corinthians 10. The wilderness generation, he says, “drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ” (verse 4). He does not mean that the stone at Horeb was Jesus; he means the Lord who gave Israel water in the desert is the Lord now known in Christ, and he warns the Corinthians not to test Christ as Israel did. Jesus' own offer of living water (John 4:10-14; 7:37-39) stands in the same line, and Hebrews 3 presses the warning of Massah on Christian readers through Psalm 95. Joshua's name, Iesous in Greek, is the same name as Jesus, and Hebrews 4:8 compares the two leaders who bring God's people toward rest. Early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr saw Moses' outstretched arms as a figure of the cross; that is a later devotional reading, not the text's own claim.

hard.q: Why does God swear to blot out the memory of Amalek and wage war on them from generation to generation?
hard.a: The oath in verse 14, repeated in Deuteronomy 25:17-19, lies behind the command in 1 Samuel 15 to destroy the Amalekites entirely, and it is among the hardest words in the Pentateuch. The text gives its reason: Amalek attacked a people just out of slavery, and Deuteronomy adds that they struck the weary stragglers at the rear and had no fear of God. Those who defend the justice of the oath stress that it is God's judgment on one people for a specific and repeated cruelty, not permission for Israel to despise foreigners, since the same Torah commands love for the stranger. Others read it within the conventions of ancient warfare, where total destruction was a standard boast (the Moabite king Mesha, around 840 BC, claimed that Israel had perished forever), and note that Amalekites appear alive in later stories. Jewish tradition came to use Amalek as a name for the persistent enemy of God's people, and Christians have generally read the war spiritually in light of Christ's command to love enemies. On each of these readings the war belongs to God rather than to Israel's appetite for revenge, which is what the altar's name confesses.

questions: The people had seen the plagues, the sea, and the manna, and still asked whether the LORD was among them. Why is past experience of God's help so easy to forget under present pressure?
Moses could not keep his hands raised alone, and Aaron and Hur held them up. Who holds up your hands, and whose hands are you in a position to hold up?
Massah became a byword for testing God. What is the difference between honestly bringing a need to God and demanding that he prove himself on your terms?
